title: Europe Is Burning: What Is the EU Doing About the Wildfires?
content:
This year’s wildfire season has already reached a massive scale. According to EFFIS data, around 576,000 hectares had burned across Europe by 17 August — an area roughly twice the size of Luxembourg. Wildfires have devastated parts of France, Spain, Greece, Portugal and Croatia, while Belgium has faced the largest wildfire in its history.

As the scale of the destruction grows, so do expectations of the European Union — along with criticism that Brussels is doing too little to prevent such disasters. But it is important to remember that the EU is not responsible for managing firefighting operations. Fighting wildfires remains primarily the responsibility of individual member states and their regional and local authorities.

The EU plays a supporting role. Under Article 196 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Brussels can support and complement national efforts to prevent disasters, prepare emergency services and respond to crises. It can also facilitate cooperation between national civil protection services. What the EU cannot do is impose a single wildfire response system on its member states.

title: Should the European Parliament Leave Strasbourg?
content:
The heart of European democracy does not beat in just one place. For historical and legal reasons, the European Parliament’s work is split across three countries.

The rules are laid out explicitly in Protocol No. 6 to the EU treaties:

“The European Parliament shall have its seat in Strasbourg where the 12 periods of monthly plenary sessions, including the budget session, shall be held. The periods of additional plenary sessions shall be held in Brussels. The committees of the European Parliament shall meet in Brussels. The General Secretariat of the European Parliament and its departments shall remain in Luxembourg.”

So how does this three-city system actually work?

Witold Naturski, director of the European Parliament Liaison Office in Poland, explains that Brussels remains the centre of the Parliament’s day-to-day legislative work.

“Twelve plenary sessions, running from Monday to Thursday, have to be held in Strasbourg each year. All the remaining work takes place in Brussels,” he says.

Brussels hosts meetings of the Parliament’s 20 standing committees, gatherings of political groups and shorter plenary sittings, sometimes referred to as “mini-plenaries.”
snippet: The heart of European democracy does not beat in just one place. For historical and legal reasons, the European Parliament’s work is split across three countries.

title: The Alps are breaking apart and glaciers are vanishing. The consequences are already economic
content:
When protective winter snow melted off Switzerland’s Alpine glaciers on 29 June 2026, marking the second earliest Glacier Loss Day in recorded history, few people paid much attention.

Winter snow acts as a shield — it reflects sunlight and protects the ice beneath. This past winter brought little of it, so it melted early, and the sun began attacking ice that had built up over centuries.

Less than two months later, the problem is far more tangible. Rivers across central Europe are running at historic lows. The loss of the Alps’ natural water reservoir is shifting from a long-term climate risk to a concrete economic problem — disrupting river transport, energy production and industrial supply chains from Bavaria to the Black Sea.

Switzerland is the continent’s natural water tower, and the rate at which it is losing glacial mass has entered a critical phase, according to Matthias Huss, head of the Swiss glacier monitoring network GLAMOS, and researchers at ETH Zürich.

title: Coffee at 330%, citrus at 85%: EU study maps what happens when banned pesticide residues are blocked from imports
content:
That is the central finding of a study by researchers at the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC).

The agency turned to this question because the Commission, in its Vision for Agriculture and Food presented last year, pledged to require imported food to meet the same standards as those applicable within the EU. “The Commission will establish a principle that the most hazardous pesticides banned in the EU for health and environmental reasons are not allowed back to the EU through imported products,” the Vision states. The executive reaffirmed this commitment this year when it presented its agricultural and food simplification package.

What the ban would cause depends first on whether growers outside the EU would choose to adapt to European standards, reduce their exports to Europe, or stop them altogether.

That was also a challenge for the authors of the analysis, which is why they estimate the consequences across three different scenarios.

The most pessimistic scenario is that producers would not stop using the banned pesticides, effectively closing the gates of the European market to them.

Agricultural imports into the EU would in that case fall by as much as 41 percent.
snippet: That is the central finding of a study by researchers at the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC).

title: EU vs NATO: Which defence clause is stronger?
content:
EU Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius was asked last month in an interview with the independent Russian outlet The Insider how likely it was that the EU could invoke the mutual assistance clause set out in Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union.

“This is an important issue. It is being discussed intensively, but not publicly — for now, mainly behind closed doors,” the Lithuanian commissioner said. He added that work was also underway on “more concrete” plans for how the provision could be put into practice.

“I think that by the end of the year we will have a clear understanding of how this article could become an equivalent of NATO’s Article 5,” Kubilius said.

Kubilius noted that when it comes to decision-making, some politicians and experts believe Article 42(7) could even prove more effective than NATO’s Article 5. Unlike NATO’s collective defence mechanism, invoking the EU clause does not require consensus among all member states.

“It also provides for what we call mutual assistance,” he said. “The country that has been attacked initiates the process itself.”

title: Inside the Kill Zone: How Drones Are Reshaping the War in Ukraine
content:
Ukrainian and Russian soldiers describe this space as a belt along the line of contact, saturated with reconnaissance equipment, dispersed infantry, isolated trenches, numerous unmanned supply vehicles and small infiltration groups. It is this zone — referred to by military analysts as the “kill zone” — where not only tactical battles are decided, but also the ability to maintain logistics and evacuate the wounded.

“The kill zone is essentially an area of increasing threat, which gradually turns into a danger zone as you move farther away from the front line. This buffer extends 7 to 10 kilometers into each side’s positions,” explains Konrad Muzyka, a military analyst and owner of Rohan Consulting. “The moment any heavy wheeled or tracked vehicle appears in this belt, FPV drones, artillery and other weapons are immediately directed against it.”

title: Disinformation fuels opposition to wind turbines in Czechia
content:
After years of planning, construction of new wind farms is finally getting under way in Czechia. But in some municipalities, projects are facing opposition from local residents, which experts say is being fuelled by disinformation about alleged health risks associated with wind turbines. According to experts, the growing influence of opponents is affecting not only decisions at local level, but also the political and development sectors.

The latest example came in early August, when a wind farm was due to be built between two municipalities in eastern Czechia. Following pressure from local opponents, who according to the fact-checking platform Evidence Ninja had been spreading false or misleading claims about the impact of wind turbines, the project was put on hold. Its future is now being discussed.

According to AMO researcher Petr Vidomus, this type of mobilisation against wind turbines is becoming increasingly common.

“Referendums on whether wind farms should be built are one indicator. Last year, the votes for and against were roughly split 50–50. This year, however, the overwhelming majority have been against them,” Vidomus says.

title: Ukraine’s internal power struggle: How the war reshaped politics in Kyiv
content:
What unfolded over several weeks in July sheds light on a system of power that, according to Dr Łukasz Adamski, director of the Mieroszewski Centre, today has more in common with the ancient concept of wartime dictatorship than with the constitutional balance between the president and parliament.

The fourth government reshuffle in Kyiv since the outbreak of Russia’s full-scale war was formally presented as a technical overhaul. As part of the reshuffle, Ukraine’s parliament approved the composition of the cabinet at the request of newly appointed Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi. 

On 16 July, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy entrusted the duties of defence minister to the head of the Security Service of Ukraine, General Yevhen Khmara. The new cabinet did not include outgoing Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov – one of the most recognisable technocrats in Ukraine’s wartime government and a politician enjoying enormous public support.

title: Torture, Violence and Death: What Ukrainian POWs Face in Russian Captivity
content:
Despite repeated prisoner exchanges, thousands of Ukrainians remain in Russian captivity, while the number of documented cases of torture and ill-treatment continues to grow. 

“If you were to ask me how severely I was tortured, I would say that on every possible scale, it was at the maximum level,” Ukrainian soldier Khuan Alberto Levya Garsiya said, describing the 1,183 days he spent in Russian captivity.

His testimony, given shortly after the Council meeting, was one of several accounts that together paint a picture of the system Russia has built around Ukrainian prisoners of war and detained civilians.

Garsiya listed the methods of torture he said he had endured with the calm precision of someone who had become familiar enough with them to name them: “daily beatings, electric shocks, exhausting exercises in freezing temperatures of minus 30 degrees Celsius, sexual violence”.

“They did everything that could be done to a person to break them psychologically,” he said.

He was, however, more fortunate than two of his fellow detainees held in detention facilities in the Donetsk region.

“They were beaten to death, and their bodies were sent back to their families in plastic bags,” he added.
snippet: Despite repeated prisoner exchanges, thousands of Ukrainians remain in Russian captivity, while the number of documented cases of torture and ill-treatment continues to grow.

title: When Disinformation Takes to the Streets and Causes Harm
content:
Six men and one woman have been remanded in custody for 30 days over an attack on an ambulance in a village in Cluj County, with the woman facing assault charges. Prosecutors said she threw a stone at the ambulance window, injuring the driver.

On Monday morning, the ambulance driver underwent a second surgery after sustaining an eye injury from shards of the shattered window.

The seven suspects stormed an ambulance with clubs, axes and stones after believing false information that had appeared on TikTok. The ambulance had picked up a patient and was taking them to hospital when it was attacked. The viral video invoked the myth of “black ambulances” – a conspiracy theory that has circulated in Romania in the past – which allegedly kidnap children.

Police identified those involved in the incident, which took place on August 8. They are aged between 18 and 44 and come from a village in western Romania.
